extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and researchers interested in mathematical pedagogy and evaluation (Russian-school perspective)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for writing, teaching, and judging mathematical theorems and expositions with emphasis on intuition, concreteness, and connection to problems (Arnold's Russian-school view). Useful for evaluating research results, proofs, and pedagogical presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness of motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem should be tied to a real problem (physical, geometric, combinatorial, computational).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold stresses that mathematics should be motivated by concrete problems rather than by fitting the world to definitions ('L'art de la définition c'est l'art de Procuste'). If a result has no interpretation as a physical/computational/geometric phenomenon it is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric / visual content
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem should have a picture; proofs admitting no diagram are suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs and statements that admit geometric or visual interpretation or a physical analog. Lack of any diagrammatic/visual content is treated as an indicator of scholastic abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to perturbation
rubrics_metrics.description: Results should not depend on hypotheses an experimentalist would never check (avoid reliance on set-theoretic minutiae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable mathematics remains true under small changes of assumptions; fragile statements contingent on pathological hypotheses are of low practical interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to old, hard problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A new theorem should say something about a previously-recognized hard problem rather than being merely formally novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold values contributions that address recognized mathematical/physical/computational difficulties over internally-novel statements inside an artificial framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance over difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty is a poor proxy for value; significance and applicability matter more than technical hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the 'self-destructive democratic principle' that rates mathematics by sheer difficulty. Emphasize meaning, applications, and insight rather than complexity for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition before formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce concepts via examples and intuition first, then provide formal definitions and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogically and aesthetically, definitions-before-examples is wrong: examples should motivate and illustrate notions before formalization. This is presented as both a teaching and aesthetic criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom-system worship (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating all axiomatic systems as equally worthy of study regardless of whether they describe anything concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold criticizes the attitude that any consistent axiom system merits equal attention; value depends on relation to concrete phenomena and problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrialised abstractness (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing theorems whose only interpretation is within the formal system that generated them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against mass-producing abstract results that exist only inside an artificial formalism and lack external interpretation or applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of attribution (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving credit to formal restatements or frameworks rather than the original discoverers of concrete phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold objects to 'shameless grabbing of discoveries from discoverers'—abstraction that erases the origin and credit of ideas is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressing dimensions and pictures (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing three-dimensional geometric intuition with n-dimensional formal manipulations from the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid starting with high-dimensional formal generalizations that remove the original geometric picture; preserve and communicate dimensional intuition where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to state without jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the theorem be stated without specialist jargon to someone in another science?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful test of concreteness: if you cannot convey the statement in nontechnical terms to an engineer or physicist, the result may be empty of concrete content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of physical or computational analogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs or statements should come with a physical analog or computational interpretation when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing a physical model or computational experiment grounds the mathematics and demonstrates relevance; absence of any analog is a strike against perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples before definitions (pedagogical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and explore examples before giving abstract definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a teaching guideline, start with concrete cases to build intuition; formal definitions should follow to capture the observed behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit original discoverers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure original discoverers are credited rather than attributing discoveries solely to later abstract reformulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly practice should acknowledge the concrete origins of ideas and their discoverers; abstraction should not erase historical attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachability test
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to teach the abstract mathematics to a bright physicist or engineer; if no concrete content can be conveyed, the abstraction is empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold proposes this as a concrete empirical test of whether an abstract theory has genuine content: successful transfer of core ideas to an applied scientist indicates meaningful mathematics.
